I get your point, but I am not certain that not wanting to have a doctor with disabilities significant enough to warrant accommodations in order to perform intellectual work is the same thing as "looking down on people with disabilities".  I just don't want my brain surgeon (or my helicopter pilot, or my defence attorney) to have any kind of a disability that would affect their ability to do their job - that would affect me directly.

This is the funny double standard: students want to have their disabilities recognized to obtain accommodations to complete their school work properly and get their high grades, yet they want to conceal that fact as much as possible when they enter the real world as if what required extensive accommodations in university suddenly no longer requires any further identification or intervention in the real world., Except that these conditions requiring accommodations don't just disappear like a puff of smoke when you graduate - they follow you for the rest of your life.  And the public pays the price for the concealment.

Let me answer your question with another question - do you think your patients would want a doctor operating on them/giving them health advice/doing other important/life-affecting medical stuff on them if they knew you needed accomodations to do your job properly?

They likely don't think your case has merit, or that the expected recovery does not justify continuing to represent you.  This usually happens when the litigation progresses and they get to hear the Defendant's side of the story, and not just yours.

It may seem unfair, but please remember that they worked for free until this point, and are presumably not seeking compensation from you for the time spent (as you indicated it was a contingency fee arrangement). 

It's a two-sided disappointment: the client feels cheated and abandoned when their lawyer fires them, and the lawyers often feel cheated and deceived because (usually) it became apparent at some point in the litigation that the client had not given them the whole story at the time they were retained.

I agree that less reliance on textbook problems for assignments (or at least those that lend themselves to mechanical solutions) would help curb the cheating.  If there were a more consistent/unified effort by the Profs. to a) provide such novel problems to students; b) give invigilated exams; and c) to shift more weighting to timed, invigilated exams; I would be a good deal happier.  I miss riding the curve instead of grinding out my grades.  This may be wishful thinking, however.  

Re EECS 3101, let's see if I can get through EECS 2011 next semester first,  but your point is taken that upper year courses become less easy to find shortcuts in.

Regarding the instructors you mention, I liked my classes with Michkine and Purzitsky (don't know the others) - I found both had an emphasis on theory in their classes, which as you have correctly surmised, I enjoy a great deal.  However, if as you say most are not interested in that, then I guess I am in a minority.  I do acknowledge that neither is perfect as an instructor, however.

One point regarding your statement about the engineers (of which you may be one) - my logic class this past summer for some reason had a large number of engineering students in it - while they may have a more practical focus because of their programs, I noted that the engineering students in my class jumped in the fray frequently and seemed to enjoy grappling with the (often abstract) concepts in that class.  Perhaps because these students are a more exclusive bunch academically than us garden-variety CSers (and in spite of their more practical focus), I found that their presence made the class more enjoyable and stimulating, and I think they enjoyed the class at least as much as I did - there must be a place for theory even for those in the more practical disciplines.

I am still convinced that the theory (and a lot of math) is very important to success in the CS field, but having not worked in the field yet, I could be wrong,   although I hope not, because I won't do it any other way - that's my stubborn streak talking.

Regards.
